docs.content:
## Mission
Studying alone in a dorm room goes worse than studying next to someone stuck on the same problem set. Quad makes that happen on purpose instead of by luck.

## What we're building
You sign in with your university email, add the courses you're taking this term, and mark the hours you're usually free: Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, or the gap between two lectures. Quad finds classmates in the same course whose free time overlaps and puts three to five of you in a group, with a suggested spot (a library room, a cafe near campus) and a recurring time. There's a group chat for rescheduling, a way to leave a group that isn't working, and no feed, no follower counts, nothing to scroll. Matching runs on two things only: same course, same hours.

## Who it's for
Students in the big courses, the intro lectures and required classes where you sit among 200 people and know nobody. It's also for people who want a study group but not a friend group: show up, work for two hours, go home.

## Where we're headed
First we want one campus where a Quad group actually meets twice a week without anyone chasing it. Then we add what makes groups stick: shared notes, a place to log what you covered, reminders that adjust when midterms hit. If it works at one school, it should work at the one down the road. Long term, we'd like to be the default answer to "who else is free right now?" on campus, without turning into another app you feel bad about not opening.

docs.title: Quad Market Research
docs.content:
# Quad Market Research

Researched 2026-10-04. Prices are the ones published or reported at that date; where a price comes from a third party rather than the company itself, I say so.

## Summary

Quad sits in a crowded field of "study with other people" products, but almost none of them do the specific thing Quad does: match you with classmates in the same course whose free hours overlap, then hand you a recurring in-person time and place. The existing players split into three camps.

1. **Body doubling and focus rooms.** Focusmate, StudyStream, Study Together, Flow Club, Kaizen. These put you next to *someone*, usually a stranger, usually online, usually not in your course. They have paying users and real scale, which proves people will pay a few dollars a month to not study alone.
2. **Course-level communities.** Coursicle automatically puts every student in a class chat, and Discord and GroupMe class servers are where a lot of actual study groups already form. They solve "find people in my course" but not "find people free when I am, and turn it into a standing meeting."
3. **Campus-sold platforms.** CircleIn, Penji, Nectir, QuadC, Mentor Collective. Universities pay, students use it free. This is where the money is in student success software, but the buyer is a provost or a learning center, not a 19-year-old.

The demand signals are strong but indirect. US postsecondary enrollment grew 1.0 percent in fall 2025 to 19.4 million students, with 16.2 million undergraduates, and community colleges grew fastest at 3.0 percent ([National Student Clearinghouse](https://nscresearchcenter.org/final-fall-enrollment-trends)). Loneliness is still widespread: 52 percent of students reported high loneliness in the 2024-25 Healthy Minds Study, down from 58 percent in 2022 ([University of Michigan](https://sph.umich.edu/news/2025posts/college-student-mental-health-third-consecutive-year-improvement.html)). Peer contact measurably helps: the Stanford coaching study found 10 to 15 percent higher retention and graduation among coached students ([Stanford GSE](https://ed.stanford.edu/news/stanford-study-shows-college-student-coaching-improves-retention-and-graduation-rates)).

The hard part is not demand, it's liquidity and payment. Matching on both course and free time needs density in a single course at a single campus, and free substitutes (Discord, GroupMe, Coursicle chats, free tiers of every focus app) are good enough for most students. Chegg went from a household name to a net loss of $103 million in 2025 and cut 45 percent of its staff to pivot away from consumer students entirely ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chegg)), which is a warning about how brutal the consumer student subscription market got once free answers existed.

## Market signals

**Enrollment is growing, and it's shifting public.**
- Fall 2025: 19.4 million total postsecondary enrollments, 16.2 million undergraduates, up 1.0 percent overall and 1.2 percent for undergrads. Community colleges +3.0 percent, public 4-year +1.4 percent, private nonprofit 4-year -1.6 percent. ([NSC Research Center](https://nscresearchcenter.org/final-fall-enrollment-trends), [Clearinghouse press release](https://www.studentclearinghouse.org/news/fall-undergraduate-enrollment-shows-overall-growth-despite-decline-at-private-colleges))
- Spring 2026: 18.6 million students, undergraduates up 1.3 percent to 15.5 million. ([NSC Research Center](https://nscresearchcenter.org/enrollment-insights))
- Reading: the first campus should probably be a big public university or a community college, not a small private one.

**Loneliness and belonging.**
- 52 percent of students reported high loneliness in 2024-25, down from 58 percent in 2022; severe depression fell from 23 to 18 percent ([U. Michigan School of Public Health](https://sph.umich.edu/news/2025posts/college-student-mental-health-third-consecutive-year-improvement.html)).
- In the same national survey, 40 percent said they lack companionship, 35 percent feel left out, 28 percent feel isolated from others ([Healthy Minds Study 2024-25 data report, PDF](https://healthymindsnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/2024-2025_HMS-National-Data-Report_Student.pdf)).
- The 2024 Student Financial Wellness Survey found 57 percent of students feel lonely sometimes or always, and lonely students had a much lower Net Promoter Score for their institution (10.9 vs 29.2) ([Trellis Strategies brief, PDF](https://www.trellisstrategies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Research-Brief_TSFEB26_Loneliness.pdf)).
- Active Minds reports 28.4 percent of students feel isolated, and lonely students are over four times as likely to report severe psychological distress ([Active Minds](https://activeminds.org/press-release/new-data-emphasizes-the-correlation-between-loneliness-and-student-mental-health)).
- This matters for Quad because belonging is the thing universities already spend money on, which makes a campus-sold version plausible later.

**Study groups are already normal behavior, just badly organized.**
- In one course-level cohort study, 78 percent of students joined at least one group study session in a semester, with a median of four sessions. Students said they showed up because a professor encouraged it or a peer invited them. ([Faculty Focus](https://www.facultyfocus.com/articles/course-design-ideas/what-students-can-learn-from-studying-together))
- Peer relationships correlate with higher GPA and higher second-year persistence ([systematic review and meta-analysis, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10800095)). The Stanford coaching study found 10 to 15 percent retention and graduation gains for coached students ([Stanford GSE](https://ed.stanford.edu/news/stanford-study-shows-college-student-coaching-improves-retention-and-graduation-rates)).
- Vendor content claims peer tutoring raised GPA 25 percent at one university ([QuadC blog](https://www.quadc.io/blog/how-a-university-increased-student-gpa-by-25-through-peer-to-peer-tutoring)). That is marketing, not peer-reviewed, so treat it as a claim.
- "Study with me" videos on YouTube were watched over 520 million times in 2023, per YouTube's own trends report as cited by Kaizen ([Kaizen](https://my-kaizen.com/virtual-study-room)). People want another human present while they work.

**Willingness to pay for accountability exists, but it's small and online.**
- Focusmate is reported at 12 million plus sessions across 150+ countries with a low seven-figure ARR, around $83K per month, on roughly $500K raised. This comes from a third-party company profile and I could not verify it against Focusmate's own numbers, so treat it as unconfirmed. ([CB Insights profile](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/focusmate))
- The consumer study-tool market is under pressure from free AI. Chegg's 2025 revenue was $376.9 million with a $103.4 million net loss; it cut 388 more staff in October 2025 and pivoted to B2B skilling ([Wikipedia, citing Chegg IR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chegg)).
- Consolidation is happening. A 2026 comparison article states StudyStream and Study Together have effectively joined forces and now point users at the same signup. Third-party claim, not confirmed on either company's site. ([Bubblic](https://www.bubblic.app/blog/best-apps-to-find-a-study-buddy-online.html))

## Competitors

Ten products plus adjacent benchmarks. "Overlap" is my read on how much they compete with Quad.

### Direct-ish: same people, similar moment

**1. Coursicle** (closest structural competitor)
- What it does: course planner for thousands of colleges, plus automatic class group chats. Enroll in a class and you're added to a chat with students in that section, with shared notes and past conversations. It calls these "instant study groups." ([Coursicle blog](https://www.coursicle.com/blog/what-is-coursicle))
- Pricing: free with premium in-app purchases listed at $4.99, $29.99 and $99.99 ([App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/coursicle/id1187418307)). Billing periods aren't stated on the listing; a review describes a $5 unlock for unlimited class tracking per semester ([Veroniiiica](https://veroniiiica.com/coursicle-class-scheduling-app-review)).
- Overlap: high on "find classmates in my course," zero on schedule matching, recurring meetings or in-person placement.

**2. StudyStream**
- What it does: 24/7 live video study rooms, cameras on, mics off, hundreds of people per room, plus streaks, Pomodoros and FocusBuddies pairing. Founded 2020 by Cambridge and King's College London graduates, YC 2021, about $2.2M raised. ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/studystream), [Tracxn](https://tracxn.com/d/companies/studystream/__iQXpDnisIek3gHSqSs_sB5hn_kYLWNIL2CJX-aHGL-E))
- Pricing: free public rooms, premium reported at about $7/month by Kaizen's September 2026 price check and about $10/month elsewhere. StudyStream's own pricing page returned no readable content when I fetched it, so treat both figures as third-party estimates. ([Kaizen](https://my-kaizen.com/virtual-study-room))
- Overlap: competes for the same "study next to someone" urge, but online and course-agnostic.

**3. Study Together**
- What it does: a large Discord-first study community with 24/7 voice and video rooms, silent study calls, leaderboards, private 1:1 and group study, 50/10 Pomodoro rooms. ([Study Together](https://www.studytogether.com), [Discord page](https://www.studytogether.com/discord))
- Pricing: the Discord server is free; the site describes free access as a deliberate choice. Reported to be well over a million members, and reportedly tied up with StudyStream as of 2026 (third-party claim). ([Bubblic](https://www.bubblic.app/blog/best-apps-to-find-a-study-buddy-online.html))
- Overlap: medium. Free, global, not course-based.

**4. Focusmate**
- What it does: books you a 1:1 video session with a stranger, 25 to 75 minutes. You state a goal, work silently on camera, check in at the end. Not subject-matched.
- Pricing: free for three sessions a week; Plus is $8/month billed yearly or $12/month monthly ([Focusmate pricing](https://www.focusmate.com/pricing)).
- Overlap: low on academics, high on "someone expects me at 7pm," which is exactly the habit Quad wants to create in person.

**5. Flow Club**
- What it does: hosted, scheduled group focus sessions, more structured and work-oriented than student rooms.
- Pricing: $40/month or $400/year, with 50 percent off for full-time students and nonprofits, so roughly $20/month for students ([Flow Club FAQ](https://www.flow.club/faq)).
- Overlap: low. Useful as a ceiling on what a premium accountability product can charge.

**6. Kaizen**
- What it does: Pomodoro timer with camera-free focus rooms. You see names, statuses and tags, no video or audio. Joining rooms is free; you need Premium to create private rooms.
- Pricing: free tier; Premium €3.99/month or €39.99/year, 14-day trial ([Kaizen pricing](https://my-kaizen.com/pricing)).
- Overlap: medium. The free-to-join, paid-to-organize split is the packaging pattern most relevant to Quad.

**7. Discord and GroupMe class servers** (the real incumbent)
- What it does: free, unmoderated-by-default chat where course-specific and subject-specific study groups already live, with Pomodoro bots and voice channels. Many university courses, clubs and exam-prep communities run their own servers. ([Bubblic](https://www.bubblic.app/blog/best-apps-to-find-a-study-buddy-online.html))
- Pricing: free.
- Overlap: very high in practice. If Quad is not faster than "someone makes a GroupMe for Chem 101," it loses. These tools are also Quad's best onboarding channel, since a group can keep scheduling in the app it already uses.

### Campus-sold (B2B) platforms

**8. CircleIn**
- What it does: virtual student community with study rooms, peer help, flashcards and task management, sold to colleges and universities. Its own pitch is explicitly "not luck and not popularity" for getting into the right study group. ([CircleIn](https://www.circleinapp.com), [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/circlein-circle-in-daily/id969803973))
- Pricing: not public. Marketing positions it as affordable for small to mid-sized institutions. Total funding reported at about $1.55M, latest round six years old, team 11-50. ([CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/myqvo), [LeadIQ](https://leadiq.com/c/circlein---the-place-for-remote-studying/5e6b5ce01d6f06b382814138))
- Overlap: high in concept, and the cautionary tale. The idea has been built and sold before without becoming large. Current activity level is unclear from public sources.

**9. Penji**
- What it does: peer tutoring and learning-center scheduling for universities. Students book peer tutors in an app; admins manage staffing and visits. Used at UGA, Rutgers, Duke, Bridgewater and others. ([Penji](https://www.penjiapp.com/tutoring))
- Pricing: custom quote, based on the number of active tutors or student visits per year ([Penji pricing](https://www.penjiapp.com/pricing)). For a sense of end-user value, Syracuse charges $25 per hour for individual tutoring booked through Penji, often covered by school vouchers ([Syracuse CLASS](https://class.syr.edu/academic-support/individual-tutoring)).
- Overlap: adjacent. Tutoring, not groups, but it owns the learning-center budget Quad would eventually ask for.

**10. Nectir**
- What it does: course chat and AI assistants for departments and institutions, LMS-integrated, FERPA and COPPA compliant. ([Nectir pricing](https://www.nectir.io/pricing))
- Pricing: department and institution plans, both "contact sales." No public price.
- Overlap: medium. It is where course-level chat is heading in a paid, institution-blessed form.

**Also worth watching, no public pricing: QuadC** (peer mentoring and student success platform for institutions, and an awkward name collision for us, [QuadC blog](https://www.quadc.io/blog/peer-mentoring-and-study-groups-the-secret-to-student-success)) and **Mentor Collective** (peer mentoring platform sold to universities, [Mentor Collective](https://www.mentorcollective.org/how-it-works)).

### Non-competitors, but pricing benchmarks

Chegg Study $15.95/month, Chegg Study Pack $19.95/month, Course Hero roughly $9.95 to $39.95/month depending on commitment, Quizlet Plus $7.99/month or $35.99/year. Sources: [Vertech Academy comparison](https://www.vertechacademy.com/blog/chegg-vs-quizlet-vs-course-hero), [Honor Society](https://www.honorsociety.org/articles/top-5-study-apps-college-students), [BookScouter](https://bookscouter.com/blog/slader-vs-chegg-study-vs-course-hero-textbook-answers). These are content and answers businesses, not matching businesses, but they set what students think a study app costs.

## Pricing signals

**Consumer band for study and focus tools: about $3 to $12 per month, with a free tier that actually works.**
- Quizlet Plus: $7.99/month or $35.99/year.
- Focusmate: $8/month annual, $12/month monthly, 3 free sessions a week.
- Kaizen: €3.99/month or €39.99/year, free to join rooms.
- StudyStream: roughly $7 to $10/month reported.
- Coursicle: $4.99 and up, with a usable free tier.
- Flow Club: $40/month, but it halves it for students, which tells you what the market will bear for students ($20).

**University email and student discounts are table stakes.** Flow Club publishes a 50 percent student discount; Quizlet, Hulu and Spotify use student verification (Hulu $1.99/month, Spotify $5.99/month via SheerID, [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/streaming/how-to-get-the-hulu-student-deal)). Quad already plans university email sign-in, which doubles as the discount gate.

**Free to join, paid to organize is the cleanest pattern.** Kaizen gives everyone free room joining and charges the host for creating rooms. Coursicle gives the planner away and charges for extras like widgets and themes. For Quad this suggests: free to be matched into a group, and charge for the things a group organizer or a heavy user wants, or sell to the campus so students never pay at all.

**B2B prices are all custom quotes.** Penji prices on tutors or visits per year; Nectir and CircleIn don't publish. Any campus deal will be a negotiation about a learning-center or retention budget, which is bigger and slower than a $5 subscription. Expect a 6 to 12 month sales cycle if Quad ever goes this way.

**What I could not find:** a public price for StudyStream from StudyStream itself, any public price for CircleIn, Nectir, QuadC or Mentor Collective, and any data on what share of students would pay for a matching product specifically. That last one is the number that matters most and it does not exist publicly.

## Risks

1. **Cold-start liquidity is the whole business.** A match needs the same course *and* overlapping free hours *at one campus*. Two hundred signups spread across five courses can produce zero matches, and the first students who get no match do not come back. Coursicle sidesteps this by only matching on course, which is always dense. Quad should either launch course by course with a stated minimum, or start with the biggest intro courses where a section has hundreds of students.
2. **Free substitutes are good enough.** Discord servers, GroupMe class chats, Coursicle's automatic class chats, and free tiers of StudyStream, Study Together, Focusmate and Kaizen all cover part of the job at zero cost. Chegg's collapse shows how fast a paid student product can lose to free alternatives.
3. **Students are the hardest audience to charge.** Subscriptions cluster at $3 to $12 a month and everything comes with a free tier. Chegg lost 45 percent of its remaining staff after failing to hold consumer subscribers.
4. **The model has been tried and stayed small.** CircleIn built almost exactly the "study rooms for your class" pitch and raised about $1.55M, with no public evidence of scale. StudyStream has raised around $2.2M. This is not proof it can't work, but it means the burden of proof is on a specific improvement (in-person, schedule-matched, recurring) rather than the category.
5. **Safety and liability for in-person meetups.** Quad sends strangers to a room or cafe at a set time. That needs reporting, blocking, public-place defaults, no home addresses, and a moderation policy before the first group meets. Universities care about this and it will come up in any campus conversation.
6. **Privacy and compliance.** Course, schedule and university email data is education-adjacent. FERPA, state privacy laws and institutional review may apply if data touches student records, and dual-enrollment high schoolers complicate it. Keep signup independent of the LMS, and keep the minimum data needed for matching.
7. **Seasonality and cohort churn.** Demand spikes at term start and midterms, and resets every semester. A group that formed in September has to survive December, and every new term is a new cold start.
8. **University dependency.** If Quad needs rosters or registrar data, integration becomes a sales project. If it doesn't, verification and trust get harder. Choose deliberately.
9. **Group decay.** Three to five strangers in a recurring slot is fragile. Without a fallback (rematch, smaller group, a leave flow that notifies the group), groups quietly stop meeting and the app looks dead.

## Sources

- National Student Clearinghouse, enrollment insights series (spring 2026): https://nscresearchcenter.org/enrollment-insights

docs.title: Product Roadmap
docs.content:
## Now

- Pick one campus and one term. Everything below depends on choosing a big public university with 200-person intro lectures, not a small private school.
- Ship a clickable match demo on the static site so a student can add two courses, mark their free hours, and watch a group of four form. It's the fastest way to find out if the idea lands before we build anything real.
- Run matching by hand for the first 30 signups. Same course, at least two overlapping free hours, groups of three to five. The spreadsheet is the algorithm until we know what people accept.
- Get five actual groups meeting in person twice a week. Nothing else in this roadmap counts until that happens.
- Talk to every person who leaves a group. Their reason is the product spec.

## Next

- Add group pages: shared notes, a log of what you covered, and reminders that shift when midterms hit.
- Let a group replace someone who dropped the course, without starting over.
- Recruit one student per large course to keep groups alive past week two. Pay them in gift cards or a free premium term.
- Test the packaging Kaizen uses: free to join a group, paid to create and control one. Run it on 50 users before touching pricing for real.
- Write down what density actually looked like (signups per course, overlap rate) so the second campus is a calculation instead of a guess.

## Later

- Second campus, same playbook, using the density numbers from the first.
- A version a learning center pays for, where students use it free. The research says universities already spend on belonging and retention.
- "Who else is free right now" for the hour between lectures. Small feature, big habit.
- Group-level premium: private rooms, longer history, export of notes.

## Owner to-dos

- Buy the domain and set up email on it (hello@ plus a reply address you'll actually check).
- Create the form backend account, Airtable or Google Sheets, and hand the agents the endpoint or API key. We can't create accounts.
- Set up a sending domain for confirmation emails so they don't land in spam.
- Pick the first campus and confirm we can name it and its course codes in public copy. Some schools are touchy about that.
- Read the library room booking policy at that campus before we suggest rooms in the app.
- Reserve handles on Reddit, Instagram and TikTok if you want a campus account.
- Decide whether the paid tier test uses Stripe or a fake checkout form. If Stripe, the account has to exist before we build the page.

docs.title: Quad Cold Start Math
docs.content:
# Quad cold start math

Researched 2026-10-04. Numbers are model estimates unless a source is linked. Everything here assumes matching only on same course + overlapping free hours, and one campus for one term, as the mission says.

## The short answer

1. **A course needs about 10 signups to reliably form a group of 3 to 5 people.** Six signups is enough for a group of 3 most of the time. Twelve to fifteen gives you two separate groups plus slack for no-shows.
2. **In block terms: you need at least 3 students free in the same 2-hour block, and about 1.5 students free in an average block.** If the busiest block in a course has fewer than 3 people, don't promise a group.
3. **At a 2 to 5 percent signup rate, those 10 signups come from one lecture of 250 to 500 students, or a course with several sections of that size.** Signup rate, not course size, is the number to watch. A 400-person lecture where the professor plugs Quad for 30 seconds is worth more than four 100-person lectures with a flyer.
4. **Recommended first campus: Texas A&M University at College Station.** Largest single-campus public in the country (74,407 students, fall 2025), 505 class sections with 100 or more undergraduates, and a state core curriculum that forces nearly every first-year student through the same four big courses. No campus has agreed to anything yet: the owner still has to confirm naming and the library room policy before we put a campus name in public copy.
5. **Fallback for the first weeks is at the bottom of this note.** Short version: shrink the group before you shrink the course or the time, run one-off sessions before recurring ones, and never show a student a dead end.

## The model

I kept it simple enough to run by hand, and I would rather be roughly right than precise.

- Divide the week into **B = 30 two-hour blocks** (Monday to Friday, 9am to 9pm, six blocks a day). Two hours is the mission's minimum overlap, so a block is a place a group can actually meet.
- Each signed-up student marks **k = 6 free blocks** (about 12 free weekday hours). k = 4 and k = 9 are the pessimistic and optimistic versions.
- The probability a given student is free in a given block is **q = k / B = 0.2**.
- **The matching pool is the whole course, not the section.** All sections of POLS 206 pool together, because the constraint is the course plus the free hours, not the room you sit in. This is a big multiplier and it's why required courses win.
- A group forms when 3 to 5 students in the same course are all free in the same block.

Expected number of blocks that can hold a group of g or more:

    E(blocks with g+) = B x P(Binomial(N, q) >= g)

where N is signups in the course. Chance that at least one such group forms is roughly `1 - e^(-E)`.

This is the classic balls-into-bins occupancy problem: students are balls, free-hour blocks are bins ([Wikipedia, balls into bins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balls_into_bins_problem)). It's the same math as hash collisions and birthday problems.

**Why this model is optimistic, in three lines.** It assumes every student's free hours are spread evenly across the whole week, which is not true (real free time clusters into lunch and afternoons). It assumes every student accepts any time they marked, including a Friday evening. And it counts students who showed up on the form, not students who will show up in the library, and matched groups always lose someone. So treat the table below as the floor and aim at two to three times it.

## The spreadsheet

Paste this into Sheets. Assumptions are on top of the table.

```csv
signups_in_course,students_per_block,blocks_holding_3plus,chance_of_at_least_one_group_of_3_5,blocks_holding_4plus,chance_of_at_least_one_group_of_4_5
3,0.6,0.24,0.21,0.00,0.00
5,1.0,1.74,0.82,0.20,0.18
6,1.2,2.97,0.95,0.51,0.40
8,1.6,6.09,0.998,1.69,0.82
10,2.0,9.67,1.000,3.63,0.97
12,2.4,13.25,1.000,6.16,1.000
15,3.0,18.06,1.000,10.59,1.000
```

Assumptions: 30 two-hour weekday blocks, 6 free blocks per student, free hours spread evenly, pool is the whole course at one campus. "students_per_block" is the average (N x k / B). "chance" is the Poisson approximation of at least one qualifying block.

Reading it:
- **3 signups: a coin flip at best.** Do not launch a course until it has more than this.
- **6 signups: 95 percent chance of a 3-person group, 40 percent chance of a 4.**
- **8 signups: near certain for a 3, 82 percent for a 4.**
- **10 signups: near certain for a 4 to 5, which is the group size the mission wants.**
- **12 to 15 signups: odds of two separate groups, which is what lets you replace someone who drops.**

Sensitivity: at k = 4 (12 free hours is too generous, students really offer 8), the 10-signup target becomes about 15 signups. At k = 9 it drops to about 7. So the honest band for "one reliable 3 to 5 person group" is **8 to 15 signups in one course**, and I'd plan on 15.

## What that means as a share of a course

| Signups needed | At 2% signup | At 5% signup | At 10% signup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 (floor, group of 3) | course of 400 | course of 160 | course of 80 |
| 15 (one reliable 3-5 group) | course of 750 | course of 300 | course of 150 |
| 30 (two groups, first-term target) | course of 1,500 | course of 600 | course of 300 |
| 45 (the roadmap's five groups, if spread over 3 courses) | 3 courses of 750 | 3 courses of 300 | 3 courses of 150 |

Two things about the roadmap fall out of this. "Run matching by hand for the first 30 signups" and "get five actual groups meeting" are the same number: 30 signups concentrated in **two or three courses** gets you five groups of 4 (each course at 10 to 15 signups), while 30 signups spread over ten courses gets you roughly nothing. Concentration is the whole game.

## Which courses hit that density fastest

**Recommended campus: Texas A&M University, College Station.**

Why it, over the alternatives:
- It is the biggest single-campus public in the country: **74,407 students at College Station in fall 2025**, 62,543 undergraduates system-wide ([Texas A&M facts](https://www.tamu.edu/about/facts.html)). One campus means one matching pool, which is exactly what cold start needs.
- **505 class sections with 100 or more undergraduates** out of 5,378 sections in fall 2025 ([Texas A&M Common Data Set 2025-2026, section I-3](https://abpa.tamu.edu/accountability-rankings/common-data-set.html), [PDF](https://abpa.tamu.edu/_files/_documents/common-data/cds-pdf-2025-2026.pdf)). Nearly one section in ten is already a 100-plus lecture, so the pool of big rooms and big courses exists without us creating it.
- **Texas law caps the problem for us.** Every bachelor's degree in Texas requires six hours of government and six hours of US/Texas history, which at Texas A&M means essentially the entire first-year cohort passes through the same four courses. A mandated course is a course that refills every term. I could not load the full core curriculum list (the catalog page truncated on fetch), so the exact codes below need a five-minute confirmation at [catalog.tamu.edu](https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/general-information/university-core-curriculum/).
- **The libraries already do what Quad needs**: reservable group study rooms described as "reservable spaces for collaborative group work" ([TAMU Libraries](https://library.tamu.edu/spaces/)). That is the suggested spot in the app, and the owner still has to read the actual booking rules before we suggest a room.
- College Station is a college town, not a commuter campus, so a recurring 2-hour slot is physically possible for most students.

Target courses, in the order I'd attack them. Pool sizes are estimates from the reasoning above, not published section counts, and the codes come from general knowledge of the TAMU catalog.

| Course | Who is in it | Pool (est.) | Signups at 3% / 8% | Clears the 15-signup target? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| POLS 206 / POLS 207 (government) | Every degree, by state requirement | Thousands a year | 30-90 / 80-240 | Yes, one lecture alone |
| HIST 105 / HIST 106 (US history) | Every degree, by state requirement | Thousands a year | 30-90 / 80-240 | Yes, one lecture alone |
| MATH 151 / 152 (engineering calculus) | All engineering and science first-years | 2,000+ | 60+ / 160+ | Yes, easily |
| CHEM 119 / 120 (general chemistry) | Engineering, pre-health, science | 1,500+ | 45+ / 120+ | Yes |
| BIOL 111 / 112 (intro biology, with labs) | Pre-health, biology, agriculture | 1,000+ | 30+ / 80+ | Yes |
| PHYS 206 / 207 (mechanics, E&M) | Engineering sequence | 800+ | 24+ / 64+ | Yes |
| ECON 202 / 203 (micro, macro) | Business and core social science | 1,000+ | 30+ / 80+ | Yes |
| PSYC 107 (intro psychology) | Core social science, popular | 800+ | 24+ / 64+ | Yes |

The pattern to copy: a course every student must take, taught in one or two giant lectures, in a term where those students are on campus with time to spare. That's the state core at Texas A&M.

**Backup campus if Texas A&M says no: Ohio State, Columbus.** 62,010 students on the Columbus campus in autumn 2026, a record 47,308 undergraduates, 8,585 new first-years ([Ohio State news](https://news.osu.edu/ohio-state-increases-total-enrollment-to-68183-students)). Ohio State's own teaching center describes a class of "700+ people" ([Ohio State Teaching and Learning Resource Center](https://teaching.resources.osu.edu/teaching-topics/teaching-large-enrollment-courses)), and third-party course data lists PSYCH 1100 sections ranging up to 630 students ([Coursicle](https://www.coursicle.com/osu/courses/PSYCH/1100)). Ohio has no state core curriculum, so the density comes from service courses (PSYCH 1100, intro chemistry and biology, calculus, econ) rather than one mandated course. Slightly harder, still very doable.

**Why not a community college first, despite the growth numbers.** Community colleges grew fastest in fall 2025, up 3.0 percent, against 1.4 percent at public four-years ([National Student Clearinghouse](https://www.studentclearinghouse.org/news/fall-undergraduate-enrollment-shows-overall-growth-despite-decline-at-private-colleges), [Community College Daily](https://www.ccdaily.com/2026/01/good-fall-enrollment-growth-but/)). The problem is shape, not size. The largest community colleges are multi-campus commuter institutions: Miami Dade College has 100,000+ students spread over eight campuses and multiple outreach centers ([MDC](https://www.mdc.edu/about/)), which leaves about 12,000 per campus, and those students are far less likely to be on campus in an open 2-hour window between lectures. A community college still fits Quad, and a single campus of one would work, but it is a harder first campus than a residential flagship. The National Student Clearinghouse data is a reason to add them in year two, not to start there.

## Fallback rule for the first weeks, while density is too low

Run this from day 1 to the end of week 3, then switch to normal matching.

1. **Shrink the group before you shrink the course or the time.** Minimum viable group is 2 or 3, and it is a real group at 2 if both people show. Never match across courses, and never match on time alone without a shared course. Those two constraints are the product.
2. **Merge blocks before you give up on a time.** If nobody shares a 2-hour block, look for a 4-hour window with 3 people free inside it and let the group pick their own 2 hours. This roughly doubles the hit rate at low signup counts.
3. **Run one-off sessions before recurring ones.** For the first meeting, propose a single 2-hour session this week, not "every Tuesday for the term". Promote it to recurring only after 3 or more people show up twice. A one-off is a much smaller ask than a semester commitment, and it tests whether the group works before anyone feels locked in.
4. **Open a drop-in hour as the floor.** Pick one fixed time and place near the big lecture halls, tell every signup in that course about it, and let whoever can come come. It's the manual version of "who else is free right now", and it gives unmatched students something to do besides wait.
5. **Show progress instead of a dead end.** Never tell a student "no match found". Tell them "CHEM 119, Tuesday 2-4: 3 of 4 seats filled, we'll confirm by Thursday". A count that goes up is a waitlist; an empty result is a churn event.
6. **Plug the lecture.** One 30-second mention in a 300-person lecture is the single biggest density lever available, bigger than any amount of flyering. This is what task #7 (email 20 instructors) is for.
7. **Kill rule: a course that has fewer than 8 signups by day 7 doesn't get a forced group.** Those students go into the drop-in hour and into the next course cohort. Never burn a student's first experience on a group of 2 at a bad time.
8. **Log every unmatched student with the two things that would have matched them** (course and block). That list is the target for the next round of recruiting, and it is the manual version of the density heat map the roadmap asks for.

## How we'll know it worked

- Match rate: share of students matched into a group of 3 or more within 7 days of signing up. Target 85 percent or better in the launch courses.
- Groups meeting twice a week by the end of week 3: the mission's stated bar is five.
- Signups per course, and the overlap rate (share of same-course pairs sharing at least one 2-hour block). Those two numbers are the density record the roadmap wants before campus two.

## Sources

- Texas A&M enrollment by location, fall 2025: https://www.tamu.edu/about/facts.html
- Texas A&M Common Data Set 2025-2026, class size (I-3): https://abpa.tamu.edu/accountability-rankings/common-data-set.html and https://abpa.tamu.edu/_files/_documents/common-data/cds-pdf-2025-2026.pdf
- Texas A&M core curriculum: https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/general-information/university-core-curriculum/
- Texas A&M Libraries, group study rooms: https://library.tamu.edu/spaces/
- Ohio State autumn 2026 enrollment census: https://news.osu.edu/ohio-state-increases-total-enrollment-to-68183-students
- Ohio State teaching center, large enrollment courses ("700+"): https://teaching.resources.osu.edu/teaching-topics/teaching-large-enrollment-courses
- Coursicle, Ohio State PSYCH 1100 section size range: https://www.coursicle.com/osu/courses/PSYCH/1100
- National Student Clearinghouse, fall 2025 final enrollment: https://www.studentclearinghouse.org/news/fall-undergraduate-enrollment-shows-overall-growth-despite-decline-at-private-colleges
- Community College Daily on the same report: https://www.ccdaily.com/2026/01/good-fall-enrollment-growth-but/
- Miami Dade College, campuses and enrollment: https://www.mdc.edu/about/
- Balls into bins (occupancy math behind the table): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balls_into_bins_problem
- Definition of a large class (students and instructors put the line around 240, instructors report maxima near 1,000): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5459251

## What I could not confirm

- Section-level enrollment for any specific TAMU course. The registrar's public schedule returned 403 and the catalog pages truncated on fetch, so the pool sizes in the table are estimates from the first-year cohort and the mandated-core logic, not counted sections. Confirming six real section sizes is an hour of work once someone can reach the class schedule from a normal browser.
- The exact TAMU core course codes. Confirm at the catalog link above before they go in any public copy.
- Whether Texas A&M's trademark office or the registrar is fine with Quad naming the campus and course codes publicly. That is a brand decision for the owner.
- Any published study of how many signups a study-group matcher actually needed. I looked and did not find one, which is why this note is a model with stated assumptions rather than a benchmark.

# Quad First Campus: Texas A&M College Station, Spring 2027

Researched 2026-10-04. This fixes the working answer to the roadmap's first item: one campus, one term, and the courses we attack first. Section sizes that I could not read off a public schedule are labeled estimates, with the exact free source to confirm them.

## The pick: Texas A&M University, College Station. Term: Spring 2027.

Texas A&M's College Station campus is the biggest single-campus public university in the country: **74,407 students on the College Station campus in fall 2025**, out of 81,354 system-wide, with 62,543 undergraduates ([Texas A&M facts](https://www.tamu.edu/about/facts.html)). One campus is one matching pool, and a matching pool is the entire product. In fall 2025 the university taught **5,378 class sections, 505 of them with 100 or more undergraduates** ([Common Data Set 2025-2026, section I-3](https://abpa.tamu.edu/accountability-rankings/common-data-set.html)). Roughly one section in ten is already a large lecture, and the university built classrooms to match: the Innovative Learning Classroom Building that opened in 2020 has ten rooms with up to 600 seats, the largest at about 600 ([KBTX](https://www.kbtx.com/2020/10/31/texas-am-university-dedicates-new-innovative-learning-classroom-building)).

The reason I would not start anywhere else is that Texas law concentrates the first-year cohort for us. Every bachelor's degree in Texas needs six hours of government and six hours of American history, and at Texas A&M that means almost the whole incoming class passes through **POLS 206, POLS 207, HIST 105 and HIST 106** ([University Core Curriculum](https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/general-information/university-core-curriculum)). Those are the same four courses the cold-start math says to aim at: a course every student must take, taught in giant sections, taken in a term when students are on campus with time to spare. College Station is a residential college town, not a commuter campus, so a recurring two-hour slot is physically possible for most students. And the libraries already do the thing the app needs to suggest: reservable group study rooms for collaborative work, which I detail below ([TAMU Libraries study rooms](https://askus.library.tamu.edu/faq/50924)).

**Why it beats the runner-up, Ohio State.** Ohio State's Columbus campus is nearly as big and its 700-person psychology lecture is a real pool, but Texas A&M wins because the state core curriculum forces essentially the entire first-year class through the same four courses, which concentrates signups in a way Ohio's service courses do not (Ohio has no required state core, so its density is spread across chemistry, biology, calculus, economics and psychology separately).

## Term dates (College Station, spring 2027)

Confirmed from the university registrar and Aggie One Stop. All times Central.

| Date | What happens | Why it matters to Quad |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nov 5-20, 2026 | Spring 2027 preregistration for continuing undergrads | Best recruiting window: students are choosing spring courses right now |
| Nov 23, 2026 to Jan 18, 2027 | Open registration | Second recruiting window; waitlists open and close with this period |
| Jan 18, 2027 | Last day to drop for a 100% refund | Signups before this may still vanish |
| **Tue Jan 19, 2027** | **First day of classes** | Launch matching this week, not earlier |
| **Mon Jan 25, 2027** | **Last day to add or drop a course (11:59 p.m.)** | Rosters settle here: the first reliable moment to hand-match |
| ~early March 2027 | Midterm season (exact grading window unconfirmed) | First stress test for group attendance |
| **Tue Apr 20, 2027, 5 p.m.** | **Last day to drop with no penalty (Q-drop)** | The drop cliff. Groups lose members here; this is when the leave/rematch flow gets used |
| Early May 2027 | Term ends, finals (exact last class day unconfirmed) | End of the pilot |

Sources: [Aggie One Stop, spring 2027 registration schedules](https://aggie.tamu.edu/my-courses-and-registration/registering-for-classes/undergraduate-registration-schedules.html), [TAMU undergraduate academic calendar 2026-2027](https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/academic-calendar).

Two things follow from the calendar. Matching should open Monday January 25, once add/drop has frozen the rosters, and the marketing push should happen in **November, while students are registering for spring**. A January launch with no November recruiting starts the term cold.

## The six intro courses to attack first

These are the six biggest intro pools, ordered by the strength of the requirement behind them. Headcounts are **model estimates, not counted sections**: I could not open the public class search (it sits behind the Howdy login), so I built these from TAMU's own class-size data (505 sections of 100-plus undergrads in fall 2025) and the core-degree requirement logic. The exact per-section numbers are free and public at [TAMU's grade distribution report](https://web-as.tamu.edu/gradereports), which lists enrollments per section, term and instructor (sections under five are hidden for privacy). Pulling these six courses there is a 15-minute job and should happen before any of these numbers appears in public copy. See the follow-up task.

| # | Course | Who is in it | Fall headcount (est.) | Typical section (est.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | POLS 206 American National Government | Every bachelor's degree (6 hrs government required by state) | 3,000-5,000 | lectures 100-400, some 500+; many sections |
| 2 | HIST 105 US History to 1877 | Every bachelor's degree (6 hrs US history required by state) | 3,000-5,000 | lectures 100-400, some 500+; many sections |
| 3 | CHEM 119 Fundamentals of Chemistry I | All engineering and pre-health first-years | 2,000-3,000 | lecture 100-250, lab 25-30 |
| 4 | MATH 151 Engineering Calculus I | All engineering and science first-years | 2,000-3,000 | lecture 60-150, plus recitations |
| 5 | BIOL 111 Introductory Biology I | Pre-health, biology, agriculture | 1,500-2,500 | lecture 150-300, plus lab |
| 6 | ECON 202 Principles of Microeconomics | All business majors, plus the social science core | 1,500-2,500 | lecture 100-300 |

Close behind and worth a seventh/eighth slot once the first six are running: **PSYC 107** (intro psychology, a core social science with a large single lecture) and **PHYS 206/207** (the engineering mechanics and E&M sequence). **ENGL 103/104** is required of everyone too and is a candidate if writing courses turn out to be bigger than the numbers above.

The point of the list is that courses 1 and 2 are the anchors. Because the state requires them, their pools refill every term with no recruiting effort in the departmental sense, and the cold-start math says a single course pool of a few thousand students clears the 8-to-15-signup target for one reliable group of 3 to 5 at any plausible signup rate (see "Quad Cold Start Math").

The six course codes and titles above are confirmed in the [TAMU University Core Curriculum](https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/general-information/university-core-curriculum) and the [course catalog](https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/course-descriptions/pols). Whether Quad may name the campus and these codes in public copy is still the owner's call, tracked as the already-open owner item.

## What the library allows for room booking

The suggested spot in the app can be a real library room today. From the libraries' own reservation system and FAQ:

- Group study rooms exist at **Evans Library, Evans Annex, the West Campus Library (WCL), and the Medical Sciences Library (MSL)**.
- Capacity ranges: **Evans groups rooms 2 to 14 people; the Annex 2 to 6**. A Quad group of 3 to 5 fits the smallest room.
- **A group may book a group study room for up to 4 hours per day.** A standard two-hour session fits inside that with room to spare.
- **Booking is online** through the library reservations system (LibCal), searchable by time, capacity and amenities (whiteboard, display monitor, outlets, Zoom-friendly).
- **You must check in** with the code in the confirmation email within 15 minutes of the start or the booking is cancelled. Quad should build the check-in into the group reminder, not leave it to the student.
- **Rooms are for academic use only.** Empty rooms may be used by anyone, but people with reservations have priority.
- Individual quiet study rooms are 8 hours per day and are explicitly off-limits to groups of two or more, so Quad should never suggest one for a group.

Source: [Evans and Annex booking page](https://tamu.libcal.com/r/search/evans-annex), [AskUs: how do I reserve a study room](https://askus.library.tamu.edu/faq/50924). The libraries also publish a full [Study Room Policies](https://library.tamu.edu/spaces/) page with the fine print (per-week booking limits, no-shows, room-specific rules). Reading that, and confirming whether Quad may book rooms on a group's behalf or must have students book, is on the owner's to-do list and still open.

## Sources

- Texas A&M enrollment by location, fall 2025: https://www.tamu.edu/about/facts.html
- Texas A&M Common Data Set 2025-2026, class size (I-3): https://abpa.tamu.edu/accountability-rankings/common-data-set.html and https://abpa.tamu.edu/_files/_documents/common-data/cds-pdf-2025-2026.pdf
- Texas A&M University Core Curriculum (government and history requirements, course codes): https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/general-information/university-core-curriculum
- Texas A&M course descriptions (POLS, HIST): https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/course-descriptions/pols and https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/course-descriptions/hist
- Texas A&M spring 2027 dates, first class day, add/drop: https://aggie.tamu.edu/my-courses-and-registration/registering-for-classes/undergraduate-registration-schedules.html
- Texas A&M undergraduate academic calendar 2026-2027: https://catalog.tamu.edu/undergraduate/academic-calendar and https://registrar.tamu.edu/academic-calendar/index.html
- TAMU Libraries study rooms FAQ: https://askus.library.tamu.edu/faq/50924
- TAMU Libraries group room booking, Evans and Annex: https://tamu.libcal.com/r/search/evans-annex
- TAMU Libraries study spaces: https://library.tamu.edu/spaces/
- Texas A&M public grade distribution report (per-section enrollment, free): https://web-as.tamu.edu/gradereports
- Third-party mirror of the same grade data, per course and professor: https://anex.us and https://grades.adibarra.com
- Innovative Learning Classroom Building, ten rooms up to 600 seats: https://www.kbtx.com/2020/10/31/texas-am-university-dedicates-new-innovative-learning-classroom-building (and the university's 2018 announcement: https://stories.tamu.edu/news/2018/04/19/texas-am-university-system-regents-approve-construction-plans-for-21st-century-classroom)
- Ohio State comparison, autumn 2026 enrollment: https://news.osu.edu/ohio-state-increases-total-enrollment-to-68183-students

## What I could not confirm

- **Exact per-section enrollment for the six courses.** TAMU's public class schedule is behind the Howdy login, and a student-maintained scraper notes the university shut down its public course-data API in 2023. The grade distribution report is the open source that gives per-section counts; I did not pull it in this pass. Treat the headcount bands as estimates until then.
- **Spring versus fall enrollment by course.** Spring at Texas A&M is smaller than fall overall (spring 2020: 64,961 total against fall 2019's 69,465), and first-year intro courses are the most fall-weighted of all. A spring launch will have smaller pools than the fall numbers imply. If the spring pilot proves the model, the real density term is **Fall 2027**, when the full incoming class hits POLS 206 and HIST 105 at once.
- **Midterm grading window and final day of classes** for spring 2027 at College Station. The add/drop and Q-drop dates are confirmed; these two are not from a primary source yet.
- **The libraries' full room policy text** (per-week booking limits, whether a group must book under one student's name). The reservation rules confirmed above are real, this is the fine print behind them.
- **Whether Ohio State is the right runner-up.** It is the prior research's second choice and I kept it; other large publics (Arizona State, UCF, Penn State) were not re-tested here.

docs.title: Quad Willingness to Pay: Plan and Interview Script
docs.content:
# Quad Willingness to Pay: Plan and Interview Script

Prepared 2026-10-04 for task #3. The question: do undergrads pay for study-group matching, and how much? Target campus: Texas A&M, College Station (the working first campus, still pending the owner's approval to name it).

This document is a plan and a script, not a result. Nobody has been interviewed yet.

## The honest limit of 10-15 interviews

Ten to fifteen conversations produce **directional signal and a list of real objections, not a price**. Three numbers to keep in view while reading the plan:

- At n=12, if half the answers go one way, the true figure could plausibly be anywhere from roughly a quarter to three quarters. The margin of error at this sample size is about ±28 points. That is fine for hearing *why*, useless for saying *what share*.
- Van Westendorp, the standard four-question price meter, is usually run on 50 to 100 potential buyers before its price intersections mean anything; Gabor-Granger wants 200 to 300 for a stable demand curve ([CleverX methods guide](https://cleverx.com/blog/pricing-research-complete-guide-to-methods-and-best-practices)). We are doing neither at this scale. We are doing qualitative discovery with a price ladder bolted on.
- People over-state what they'll buy when the thing is hypothetical. That gap between stated and actual purchase is the documented weakness of every direct price question ([SurveyMonkey on Gabor-Granger vs Van Westendorp](https://www.surveymonkey.com/market-research/resources/gabor-granger-vs-van-westendorp)). The only signal that isn't a claim is money actually changing hands.

So the deal with ourselves: this round tells us whether the price question is even alive, and what the free-versus-paid story sounds like. A real number needs the follow-up survey in the last section.

## What desk research already says

Re-searched on 2026-10-04. I found no public study of willingness to pay specifically for schedule-based study-group matching, which matches the conclusion in "Quad Market Research." What exists is adjacent:

- **The consumer band for study and focus apps is about $3 to $12/month, with a free tier that actually works.** Focusmate $8/month annual ($12 monthly, 3 free sessions a week), Kaizen €3.99/month, Quizlet Plus $7.99/month, StudyStream reported around $7 to $10/month, Coursicle $4.99 and up ([Quad Market Research](https://www.focusmate.com/pricing), [Kaizen pricing](https://my-kaizen.com/pricing)). Everything comes with a usable free version.
- **"Free to join, paid to organize" is the packaging pattern that fits Quad** (Kaizen charges the host who creates a room, not the people joining). The roadmap's Next item already adopts this.
- **Students already pay for plenty of subscriptions, and forget about some of them.** US adults average $90/month on subscriptions, with $17/month spent on ones they don't use; Gen Z waste the most, $23/month on average ([CNET subscription survey, June 2025](https://www.cnet.com/tech/services-and-software/subscription-survey-2025)). That says the money exists; it does not say students will spend it on Quad.
- **The alternative to paying is a campus paying.** Universities frame peer support and belonging as retention spend, and retention is worth real money to them (1 to 3 points of retention is framed as millions in preserved tuition, e.g. [QuadC's own blog](https://www.quadc.io/blog/retention-quantifying-the-financial-value-of-student-success-technology), which is vendor marketing, not research). That is why we test a free-to-the-student, campus-paid option in the script.

The one number that matters most, the share of students who'd pay for matching specifically, still does not exist publicly. That is the point of doing this ourselves.

## The plan

**Who to talk to (12-15 undergrads, one campus).** Recruit for spread, not convenience:

- At least 8 who are currently taking or recently finished one of the launch courses: POLS 206, HIST 105, CHEM 119, MATH 151, BIOL 111.
- At least 4 first-years (new to campus, the loneliest cohort and the one that fills those lectures).
- At least 3 who study alone today and have never joined a group. They are the hardest to find and the most informative.
- Avoid recruiting only friends of the team. People who want to please you give you the answer you want, which is exactly the failure the Mom Test is written about ([Mom Test summary](https://www.koji.so/blog/mom-test-customer-interviews-2026)).

**How to recruit.** Outside those lecture halls, in course GroupMes and Discords, and through one student club. Any message that goes to students is outward-facing and needs the owner's review before it's sent.

**How to run each one.** 20-25 minutes, one interviewer, audio recorded with permission, or a two-person setup (one asks, one takes notes). Say up front that it isn't a sales pitch and that you work on the project. The interviewer should talk less than a fifth of the time.

**How to analyze.** Tag every transcript for: (a) whether and how a group forms today, (b) what breaks, (c) money already spent on study help, (d) reaction to the concept, (e) the price-ladder answers, (f) reaction to campus-paid. Then count themes and report counts as raw numbers ("9 of 13 said X"), never as percentages of a population.

## The 10-question interview script

Rules for the interviewer: ask about what actually happened, not what they'd do in a made-up future. Don't describe Quad until question 7. Don't defend the idea when they push back. When they give an opinion, ask for the story behind it.

**Warm-up (not counted, ~2 min).** "Thanks for the time. I'm not selling anything. I'm trying to understand how studying with other people actually works for you, good and bad. Is it OK if I record this? Nothing goes out with your name on it."

**1. Walk me through the last time you studied with other people for a class. Which course, who was there, and who set it up?**
Probe: How did you all end up in the same place? Did it happen again?
(If they've never done it, ask instead: last time you were stuck on a problem set late at night, what did you do?)

**2. When you're stuck at 9 p.m. on a problem set, who do you actually message, and where?**
Probe: A friend, a class GroupMe, a Discord, a TA, a search engine, nobody? How long until someone answers?

**3. Tell me about a study group you were in that stopped meeting, or never really got going. What happened?**
Probe: Who decided to stop? Did anyone say anything? Have you tried since?

**4. Where do you usually study on campus for your hardest course, and how did you pick that spot?**
Probe: Have you ever booked a library room? How did that go?

**5. What do you already pay for every month that helps with school or getting things done? Roughly what does each cost, and how long have you had it?**
Probe: Which of those do you actually still use? Which one do you keep meaning to cancel?
(Purpose: real spending, past and current, not hypothetical.)

**6. The last time you studied with classmates, what did you get that you wouldn't have gotten alone? And what was the annoying part?**
Probe: What made it worth it, or not worth it, in time?

**7. Read this and tell me what you think. [Read the concept card in 30 seconds: sign in with your university email, add your courses, mark the hours you're free; Quad puts you in a small group of classmates in the same course who are free at the same time, with a place and a recurring time. No feed, nothing to scroll.]**
Probe: What sounds useful? What sounds like it wouldn't work for someone like you?

**8. Four quick numbers. For a monthly Quad subscription: at what price would it be so cheap you'd doubt it actually works? At what price is it a bargain? At what price does it start to feel expensive? At what price is it too expensive to consider?**
(Mom Test note: this is the one deliberately hypothetical question, so treat it as the weakest data in the set. Record the four numbers per person and look for a range, not a point.)

**9. Price ladder. For each monthly price, tell me whether you'd sign up today: free ($0); $3; $5; $8. Then separately, if it cost you nothing because Texas A&M paid for it, would you feel differently about it, and would you use it any differently?**
Probe on each: what would make you pick this up, or not? Push back once on a "yes" to see if it holds ("really, $8 a month, out of your own money?").

**10. If a Quad group for [their course] could meet next week at a time you're already free, would you join? Would you put $3 down today to hold a spot? Why or why not? What would have to be true for you to say yes?**
(Purpose: the $3 deposit is the closest thing to a behavioral test we can run in a conversation. Even so, unless money actually moves, it's a claim, not proof.)

**Close.** "Anything I should have asked? Who else should I talk to who might see it differently?"

## How we log what we hear

Every answer is a claim by a student, not a fact about the market. In the readout, write "six of twelve said they'd pay $5" and "three said they'd only use it if it were free." Do not write "students will pay $5." Any number from this round carries the sample-size caveat from the top of this document.

One durable thing to watch for and record: real, already-spent money on study help (a tutor, a paid notes app, a Quizlet subscription). That is the only evidence in the set that isn't a hypothetical.

## What we'd do with the answer

- If a majority would pay $3 to $5 and few balk at $5, the next test is a real paywall at $5 on the first matched cohort, not another survey.
- If most people insist on free or campus-paid, the "learning center pays, students use it free" idea stops being a Later item and moves up. That is a slower, bigger sale, so it's better to learn now than after building a consumer paywall.
- Either way, once we have the interviews, a proper 100-plus respondent survey (Van Westendorp plus a Gabor-Granger ladder at $0, $3, $5, $8, campus-paid) is the shortest path to a defensible number. See the follow-up task.

## Owner actions this needs

- Any recruiting message to students goes out only after the owner reviews it.
- Live conversations with students are human work. Someone human runs these, either the owner or a student helper. Bots can draft the recruiting message and turn this script into a self-serve online form, but they can't hold the conversation.
- If we offer a small e-gift-card incentive to get 12-15 responses, that spend is the owner's call. An ask is filed separately.

## Sources

- Quad Market Research and Quad Cold Start Math (internal, 2026-10-04)
- Focusmate pricing: https://www.focusmate.com/pricing
- Kaizen pricing: https://my-kaizen.com/pricing
- CNET subscription survey, June 2025 (US adults $90/month; $17/month unused; Gen Z $23/month): https://www.cnet.com/tech/services-and-software/subscription-survey-2025
- CleverX pricing methods guide (Van Westendorp 50-100, Gabor-Granger 200-300): https://cleverx.com/blog/pricing-research-complete-guide-to-methods-and-best-practices
- SurveyMonkey, Gabor-Granger vs Van Westendorp (stated-versus-actual gap): https://www.surveymonkey.com/market-research/resources/gabor-granger-vs-van-westendorp
- Mom Test principles (ask about past behavior, not hypotheticals): https://www.koji.so/blog/mom-test-customer-interviews-2026 and https://www.sachinrekhi.com/p/the-mom-test-rob-fitzpatrick
- QuadC on retention value of student success tech (vendor claim): https://www.quadc.io/blog/retention-quantifying-the-financial-value-of-student-success-technology

## What I could not confirm

- Any published willingness-to-pay figure for schedule-based study-group matching. I looked again and found none, so this remains primary-research-only.
- Whether the campus-paid option is realistic at Texas A&M specifically. The retention-spend argument is general and most of the sources for it are vendors selling to universities, not neutral research.
- That 12-15 interviews will include enough students who currently study alone. If recruiting through course chats, the respondents will skew toward students who already self-organize; the plan says to compensate, but it may not be fully possible.

docs.content:
# Quad manual matching pilot: two weeks, one cohort

One operator, up to 30 signups, two or three courses, one campus. This page is the whole procedure.

## Scope and dates

- **Cohort:** the first 30 qualified signups in the launch courses. Two or three courses only: POLS 206, HIST 105, CHEM 119 at Texas A&M College Station (the working first campus). Signup 31 waits for cohort two, or takes an opening when someone leaves a group.
- **Window:** Monday Jan 25 to Sunday Feb 7, 2027. Rosters stop moving at the add/drop deadline (11:59 p.m. Mon Jan 25), so matching opens that Monday.
- **Day 0** means the day a group's first email goes out, not the day the pilot opens. From there every group runs the same 14 days. If the term or campus changes, shift every date by the same number of days.

## Have these ready before day 0

1. Signup rows in the sheet. If the sheet isn't wired yet, the confirmation email already asks students to reply with their hours, so the inbox is the backup intake.
2. A library room link (LibCal, group rooms at Evans or the Annex) and someone who has read the room policy. Open owner item: whether Quad books for a group or each student books their own.
3. One drop-in hour: a fixed weekday time in a public spot near the big lecture halls, for everyone who isn't matched.
4. Sending from •••@nightshift-demo.example. No founder address is set up yet.
5. Campus name and course codes stay out of public copy until the owner approves naming. The group email names a course and a spot, both of which the student already has, and never names the university.

## 1. Intake

Work each signup in this order.

1. **Qualify.** University email on the campus domain, plus at least one course on the launch list. Everyone else stays on the waitlist with one line back: "We're not at your school yet, you're on the list." Nothing more.
2. **Get the hours.** If free hours are blank, reply within 24 hours: "What hours are you usually free on weekdays? Rough is fine, for example Tuesdays and Thursdays 2 to 5." No hours means no match.
3. **Turn hours into blocks.** The week is 30 two-hour blocks, Monday to Friday, 9am to 9pm (9-11, 11-1, 1-3, 3-5, 5-7, 7-9). One block is the minimum overlap, which is the same thing as two overlapping free hours. "Tuesday and Thursday 2 to 5" becomes two blocks a day, 1-3 and 3-5.
4. **Log it.** One row per signup: date, name, email, courses, hours as typed, blocks, status, group, block, notes. Status is one of new, incomplete, matched, queued, dropped.

Cutoff for cohort one is 30 qualified signups. Hold the overflow for cohort two.

## 2. The matching rule

Two conditions, both required: **same course**, and **at least one shared two-hour block**. The pool is the whole course, every section together, not the section a student sits in.

For each course:

1. Count students per block. Every block with 3 or more unmatched students is a candidate.
2. Take the busiest candidate block. Cap it at 5 people.
3. Tie-break: a Mon, Tue or Wed slot first, then a slot ending by 5pm, then the earlier hour. That puts both meetings inside the window with a check-in after each one.
4. Repeat until no block has 3 unmatched students left.

An example. POLS 206 has 11 signups. Four are free Tue 2-4, three are free Thu 11-1, two are free Mon 5-7, two are free Fri 3-5. Group A is Tue 2-4 with four people. Group B is Thu 11-1 with three. The Mon and Fri pairs are not groups. Both pairs get the drop-in hour and stay queued for a third signup in their block.

Never match across courses. Never match on time alone. A pair is not a group. A block of 2 is not a group.

## 3. Group size

Three to five people. Four is the target. Never 2, because a pair cancels easily. Never 6, because the sixth person starts a second group. Cap a group at 5; the next student in that block goes into a second group in another block that works for them, or waits with a spot in the drop-in hour.

## 4. Where groups meet

Default to a bookable library group study room. Evans and the Annex have rooms for 2 to 14 people, so 3 to 5 fits, and a room can be booked for up to 4 hours a day, which covers a 2-hour session. Someone has to check in with the code in the confirmation email within 15 minutes of the start or the room is released. Put that line, the room link and the check-in rule in the group email.

If no room is free, fall back in this order: library annex tables past the periodicals, student center long tables by the north entrance, the engineering building atrium, then a cafe near campus. Public places only. Never a home address, a residence hall room, or a cafe after 8pm. Never suggest an individual quiet study room, because those are off limits to groups.

## 5. The first message each group gets

Send one email to all members, as a single thread they can reply-all on. Until the in-app group chat exists, that thread is the group's channel.

> Subject: Your Quad group for POLS 206, Tuesdays 2 to 4pm
>
> Hi Maya, Deion, Priya and Sam,
>
> You four are all in POLS 206 and all free Tuesday 2 to 4pm, so you're a Quad group.
>
> First meeting: Tuesday Jan 27, 2 to 4pm, group study room, Evans Library 2nd floor. Book a 2-hour room here and check in with the code in your confirmation email within 15 minutes, or the room gets released: [LibCal link]
>
> Bring whatever you're working on. The idea is two hours of work next to people on the same problem set, then go home. You don't have to talk the whole time.
>
> If the time stops working, reply to this and we'll fix it. If you want out, tell us and you're out.
>
> Reply "in" so we know this landed.
>
> The Quad team

Send it within 24 hours of building the group.

## 6. Check-ins

Two per group, one question each, sent after the meeting rather than before. No reminder emails in between. That gap is what makes the success metric mean something.

**Day 4, after the first scheduled meeting.**

> Subject: Did the group meet?
>
> Did the four of you meet this week? Reply yes or no. If it didn't happen, one line on what got in the way is all I need, and I'll change the time or the group.

**Day 10, after the second scheduled meeting.**

> Subject: Did you meet again?
>
> Did you meet a second time this week, without me chasing you? Reply yes or no. If the time or the mix of people isn't right, say so and I'll redo it once.

Log both answers. If day 4 is no, one repair only: re-time the group or move the person. If day 10 is no, that group is over and its members hear it plainly: "This group isn't meeting, so I'm taking it apart. Here's the drop-in hour, and I'll put you in a new group next round."

## 7. What makes us stop

- **Course floor.** A course with fewer than 8 signups by day 7 gets no group. Those students go to the drop-in hour and stay queued. Never spend a student's first experience on a forced group.
- **Group floor.** A group where fewer than 3 people show at the first meeting does not get a second meeting scheduled. The survivors get one re-match offer.
- **Pilot floor.** Fewer than 3 groups have met twice by the end of day 14, or fewer than 15 signups arrived in total: stop manual matching for this cohort, write down why, and fix that before running another. If the problem was density, the answer is recruiting, not the matching rule.
- **Safety.** If a member says they're uncomfortable, gets unwanted contact, or is repeatedly left alone, cancel that group's next meeting and move the person. Nothing meets in a private place while Quad has no block or report tool.

## 8. Success metric

A group succeeds when it meets twice with no reminder from us: the same group, at the agreed time and place, 3 or more members present at the second meeting, and no logistical reminder sent by Quad between meeting one and meeting two. The setup email and any answer to a question the group raised themselves don't count against it. The day 4 and day 10 emails are questions asked afterwards, not reminders.

Target: 5 groups. Keep going at 3 or more.

## The two-week clock

| Group day | What the operator does |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Build the group, send the first email |
| 1-4 | First meeting happens |
| 4 | Check-in 1 |
| 7 | Course floor check; close any course under 8 signups |
| 7-11 | Second meeting happens |
| 10 | Check-in 2 |
| 14 | Tally: groups matched, groups that met twice, and the reason for every group that didn't |

## Owner items this plan waits on

Room booking policy at the launch campus, the sheet endpoint or API key, the confirmation email and its sending domain, and approval to name the campus and course codes in public copy.
